meta.title: Who really said "There has always been a saying in baseball that you can't make a hitter, but I think you can improve a hitter. More than you can improve a fielder"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Ted Williams really said it — to reporters at Fenway on his last day, printed by Ed Linn in SPORT, February 1961. Not from The Science of Hitting.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There has always been a saying in baseball that you can't make a hitter, but I think you can improve a hitter. More than you can improve a fielder'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine, and precisely locatable: Williams's answer to a reporter at Fenway Park in 1960, printed by Ed Linn in SPORT magazine, February 1961.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder, the last man to bat .400
answer.sourceLine: Williams said it at Fenway Park on his last day as a player, answering a reporter Linn names only as Chase, who had reminded him he was about to become a batting coach; Ed Linn printed the exchange in his SPORT magazine account “The Kid’s Last Game” (February 1961), reprinted with the dialogue intact in at least eight later anthologies. The headline form is how the line circulates; Linn sets it as two sentences, and his full four-sentence answer is quoted in the source panel. It does not come from The Science of Hitting.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Ed Linn (1922–2000), sportswriter, quoting Williams directly
The Third Fireside Book of Baseball (1968); The Best of Sport, 1946–1971 (1971), p. 186

source.excerpt:
Chase reminded Ted that he was scheduled to become a batting coach. “Can you take a .250 hitter and make a .300 hitter out of him?”
“There has always been a saying in baseball that you can’t make a hitter,” Ted answered. “But I think you can improve a hitter. More than you can improve a fielder. More mistakes are made in hitting than in any other part of the game.”
At this point Williams was literally encircled by photographers, amateur and pro…
trail: The specialists have not claimed it. A site search of Quote Investigator ↗ turns up no article on this line, and Wikiquote’s Ted Williams page ↗ does not carry it in any section — so the sourcing had to be built from the printed record.

The words are there in print, verbatim. Open Library’s full-text search ↗ returns the sentence from The Third Fireside Book of Baseball, The Best of Sport, 1946–1971, The Ted Williams Reader, Impossible Dreams and Ed Linn’s own biography, all reprinting the same article.

And so is the question that prompted it. Searching the line before Williams’s answer recovers the setup — “Chase reminded Ted that he was scheduled to become a batting coach” ↗ — which fixes the remark to Linn’s account of Williams’s last day at Fenway Park.

The article’s own credit line closes it. Glenn Stout’s headnote ↗ introduces the piece as “from Sport, February 1961,” and the Fireside acknowledgments ↗ credit “Ed Linn and Sport Magazine for ‘The Kid’s Last Game,’ © 1961 by the Macfadden-Bartell Corporation.”
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the reprints of Linn’s article rather than from the magazine: the February 1961 issue of SPORT is not digitised, so the text here is what eight independently scanned anthologies print, read through Open Library’s full-text index. “Chase” is how Linn names the man who put the question — one of the press pack around Williams that afternoon; the article gives him no more introduction than that.

author.name: Ted Williams
author.heading: The man who said it
author.metaLine: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder · .406 in 1941 · Hall of Fame, 1966
author.bio: Ted Williams spent his whole major-league career with the Boston Red Sox, won six batting titles and two Triple Crowns, and in 1941 hit .406 — still the last .400 season in the majors. Two stretches of his prime went to the Marine Corps: a flight instructor in the Second World War, a combat pilot in Korea. He homered in his final at-bat on 28 September 1960, was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1966 in his first year of eligibility, and later managed the Washington Senators.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with it
misattribution.intro: Nothing here is fabricated — the wording is Williams’s own, on the record. What travels badly is the sourcing, a word dropped from the last sentence, and one anthology’s rewrite.

items.who: AZQuotes, and the aggregators downstream of it
items.why: AZQuotes ↗ attaches no publication to the line at all — its stated source is IMDb’s ‘Personal Quotes’ list. That is the provenance behind most web copies: an aggregator citing an aggregator, never the 1961 article.

items.who: AZQuotes, BrainyQuote and the copies downstream of them
items.why: The web copies do carry the closing sentence — but a preposition falls out of it. AZQuotes ↗ and BrainyQuote ↗ both print “More mistakes are made hitting than in any other part of the game.” The reprints of Linn’s article read “made in hitting” ↗, which is the version to quote.

items.who: The Gigantic Book of Baseball Quotations
items.why: Wayne Stewart’s collection welds two sentences into one — “you can improve a hitter more than you can improve a fielder” — which turns a flat statement plus an aside into a single comparative claim. Linn prints them as separate sentences, as the two wordings side by side ↗ show. In fairness, the headline form at the top of this page compresses too, in its own smaller way — the verbatim text is set out above.

items.who: Williams's hitting manual, The Science of Hitting
items.why: The line is often taken for book wisdom, but it is not in the book. Open Library’s full-text index covers The Science of Hitting — the book surfaces for other phrases from its pages — yet it never appears among the results for any phrase of this quote, and Goodreads’ quote page for the book ↗ does not carry it either.

misattribution.truthLine: The real citation is Ed Linn, “The Kid’s Last Game,” SPORT, February 1961 — reprinted with the exchange intact in The Best of Sport, 1946–1971 ↗ and The Third Fireside Book of Baseball ↗.

context.heading: Why he was being asked
lead: The question was not philosophical. Williams had just played his last game and had agreed to come back the following spring as the Red Sox batting coach, and a reporter in the scrum around him wanted to know what that job was actually worth: Can you take a .250 hitter and make a .300 hitter out of him? The famous line is the first half of a working coach’s answer — a man declining to promise miracles while refusing to accept that nothing can be taught.

The reasoning is the half nobody quotes. Williams did not simply say hitting can be improved; he said why — because hitting is where the mistakes are, and a discipline full of mistakes is a discipline with room in it. Pulled off the page as a one-line motto, it reads as vague encouragement. Taken whole, it is a claim about where coaching effort actually pays.
context.detailsSummary: The reprint chain, book by book
detailsBody: Linn’s article travelled further than most magazine journalism. It was anthologised in The Third Fireside Book of Baseball (Charles Einstein, 1968) and again in The Baseball Reader: Favorites from the Fireside Books of Baseball; in The Best of Sport, 1946–1971 (Al Silverman) and The Twentieth Century Treasury of Sports; in Sport Magazine’s All-Time All Stars (Tom Murray); in The Ted Williams Reader and Ted Williams: Reflections on a Splendid Life (Lawrence Baldassaro); and in Glenn Stout’s Impossible Dreams: A Red Sox Collection. Linn later reused the scene in his own biography Hitter: The Life and Turmoils of Ted Williams.

The reprints preserve the exchange word for word, which is how the wording can be checked without the magazine: the same sentences appear in eight separately scanned books, and the small divergences between them are optical-recognition noise rather than editorial change.

sourcesVerified.claim: The sentence "More than you can improve a fielder. More mistakes are made in hitting than in any other part of the game." appears in scans of The Third Fireside Book of Baseball, The Best of Sport 1946-1971, The Ted Williams Reader, Impossible Dreams and Ed Linn's Hitter.

The remark answers the question "Can you take a .250 hitter and make a .300 hitter out of him?", asked after "Chase reminded Ted that he was scheduled to become a batting coach" — the reprints name Chase, not "someone".
Glenn Stout's Impossible Dreams introduces Ed Linn's "The Kid's Last Game" as "from Sport, February 1961".
The Third Fireside Book of Baseball acknowledges "Ed Linn and Sport Magazine for 'The Kid's Last Game,' © 1961 by the Macfadden-Bartell Corporation".
The Best of Sport, 1946-1971 lists "The Kid's Last Game • Ed Linn" beginning at page 186, and other anthologies list the same article by Ed Linn.
The Gigantic Book of Baseball Quotations prints the run-on variant "you can improve a hitter more than you can improve a fielder", unlike the anthology reprints which keep the two sentences separate.

Ted Williams was born 30 August 1918 and died 5 July 2002; he played only for the Boston Red Sox, hit .406 in 1941 as the last player to bat .400, won six batting titles, two Triple Crowns and two MVPs, served as a Marine pilot in the Second World War and Korea, homered in his final at-bat on 28 September 1960, was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1966 in his first year of eligibility, and later managed the Washington Senators.
Ed Linn (1922-2000) was an American sportswriter who wrote extensively on baseball, including Hitter: The Life and Turmoils of Ted Williams.
Wikiquote's Ted Williams article does not carry this quote in any section.
Quote Investigator has no article on this quote; a site search for "make a hitter" returns only unrelated pieces.
AZQuotes prints the quote and gives its source as IMDb's Biography/Personal Quotes page, with no book, date or publication.
Goodreads' quotes page for The Science of Hitting does not include this quote.
